newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Cadbury profits up, mulls acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Cadbury profits up, mulls acquisitions.

text.p: British sweets and soft drinks group Cadbury Schweppes Plc reported a 16 percent increase in annual profits on Wednesday and said it might hit the acquisition trail using cash from the sale of its stake in Coca-Cola & Schweppes Beverages.
The company said strong performances from both confectionery and beverages helped to drive up profits, which were at the top of market expectations.
Pretax profits rose to 592 million pounds ($955.4 million) from 511 million, on sales of 5.12 billion, up from 4.78 billion. The dividend was increased by six percent to 17 pence a share.
The shares, down five pence to 505 pence, suffered from profit-taking after the stock set a three-month high on Tuesday.
Chief executive John Sunderland said the group had performed strongly across the whole range of the group's businesses.
"We regard it as a strong year. It's good for us that it's across both our beverages and our confectionery businesses and most of our markets performed very well," he said in an interview.

Sunderland said Cadbury would look at the possibility of making acquisitions using the 623 million pound proceeds from the sale of its 51 percent share in Coca-Cola & Schweppes Beverages completed last month.

The money would give Cadbury lots of options to develop its brands organically both in soft drinks and confectionery. The company could also "acquire any appropriate businesses that we see, be it in beverages or I guess more likely in confectionery", he told Reuters.
In soft drinks in North America, Dr Pepper achieved four percent growth by volume and its overall growth outpaced the market as it has done for the last decade.

But Sunderland acknowledged that competition was fierce. Cadbury's 7 Up was only now stabilising after many years of decline. Sales of 7 Up concentrate were ahead so far in 1997 compared with a year ago.
Sunderland said 7 Up's market share was slightly down in 1996 by about 0.3 percentage points, but Dr Pepper gained share.
European soft drinks suffered from a poor summer in northern Europe, with most markets flat or down.
"It wasn't a great year in Europe in the volume sense although ... all of our European markets in beverages in profit terms were up with the exception of Portugal," Sunderland said.

In Britain, the soft drink market was down slightly against the very hot summer in 1995. But Coca Cola & Schweppes Beverages profits were up three percent, which Cadbury considered very satisfactory give the outstanding summer in 1995.

In confectionery, all Cadbury's core companies had a good year. In Britain Cadbury Ltd increased market share for the third year in a row, driven by product innovation. Fuse, launched in September, was in the top three selling chocolate bar brands in Britain along with Mars and Kitkat, Sunderland said.
Sunderland was sceptical about recent speculation that Anglo-Dutch consumer products group Unilever Plc might make a bid for Cadbury.

Unilever's plans to sell its speciality chemicals business prompted suggestions that it might bid for Cadbury, but investment analysts have been dismissive about the takeover talk. Sunderland said, "It's not for me to comment, but I'm quite prepared to say that I share the scepticism." ($ = 0.619 British Pounds)
